newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FEATURE - Mercosur sparks new car goldrush in South America.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Mercosur sparks new car goldrush in South America.

text.p: Carmakers are pouring billions of dollars into South America's Mercosur trade bloc to secure their grip on one of the world's fastest-growing markets but newcomers are also seeking a share of the action.
Fiat, Ford, General Motors and Volkswagen say they will spend some $15 billion over the next four years to beef up output in a region expected to become the world's fifth-largest car market by 2000.
"We have to strengthen our positions now," said Jose Favaretto, corporate relations director for Fiat do Brasil, which has been in the country for 20 years.
Mercosur car production is concentrated in Argentina and Brazil, South America's two largest economies.
Fiat, Ford, GM and Volkswagen have long dominated both markets, benefiting from protectionist trade policies in the two countries.
From Argentina and Brazil, the four car manufacturers export cars duty free to Mercosur partners Paraguay and Uruguay, where they have carved up the market primarily among themselves.
BOOMING MARKET ATTRACTS NEWCOMERS
But the lifting of import restrictions and changes in policy over the past few years have attracted a host of new car makers to the two countries.
The new arrivals hope to take advantage of a surge in middle-class car buying -- prompted by regional inflation-slashing drives -- and strong growth prospects.
In the past two years, Toyota Motor Corp, Honda Motor Corp, Renault SA, Chrysler Corp, Daimler-Benz's Mercedes and Asia Motors have opened new factories in the region or announced plans to do so.

Newcomers are eyeing a market that is expected to grow by 10 to 15 percent a year over the next four years. By comparison, car demand in Europe and the United States has dwindled to about two percent a year, analysts said.

"Automakers hoping to survive in the global market must produce a minimum of three million cars a year and they're rushing to developing nations to secure market share and reach this target," said S. Stefani, director of Autodata, Brazil's automobile industry newsletter.

By 2000, annual car output in Mercosur is expected to grow to 3.5 million units, with 2.5 million from Brazil and one million from Argentina. Today, Brazil produces 1.7 million cars a year and Argentina makes 500,000.
If the growth forecasts hold, Brazil is set to replace Italy as the world's ninth-largest car maker before the year 2000, analysts say.
In addition to strong local demand in Mercosur, which groups 200 million consumers, new and established carmakers see the region as a platform for exporting cars to other markets.

"The presence here is very important not only because it is a dynamic market, but also because it is a platform to other Latin American countries, South Africa and Eastern Europe," Fiat's Favaretto said.
COMPETITION SEEN REPLACING "WAGONS" WITH QUALITY CARS

Analysts welcome the new arrivals to South America's car market, noting that the increasingly competitive environment is long overdue. For years, the region's leading four car makers were criticised for making inefficient and expensive vehicles while virtually being guaranteed sizeable market share without the threat of outside competition.
Former Brazilian president Fernando Collor, who left office in 1992, was angered by the outdated models the four companies put on the Brazilian market, and referred to the vehicles as "wagons".
To shake up the domestic market, Collor dramatically reduced import tariffs, which resulted in a flood of imports and huge trade deficits, forcing successive governments to restore heavy duties.
In 1995, President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's administration adopted Brazil's current car import policy.
The policy allows car manufacturers with production plants in Brazil to import cars at a 35 percent duty, while imports from carmakers without a Brazilian operation are levied a 70 percent duty.

The tariff policy has been sharply criticised by the U.S., Japanese, South Korean and European governments, which have called it protectionist. But it has succeeded in drawing new carmakers to Brazil, one of the government's main objectives.
Argentina has also relaxed import restrictions over the past few years, opening the market to new companies and helping to boost car output from 100,000 units in 1990 to 500,000 today.
BETTER CARS FOR BETTER PRICES

Most observers say the heightened competition will lower prices and improve the quality of cars available to South Americans. In the past two years, Volkswagen and Fiat have built plants in Brazil that are as technologically advanced as their facilities in Europe. The plants have dramatically cut labour costs while raising quality control standards and output.
"By the year 2000, each of the four automakers will have an installed output capacity of 900,000 cars a year. The price trend will naturally drop," Autodata's Stefani said.
The four established firms are also reorganising their existing production facilities in Brazil and Argentina to cut production and transport costs by bringing certain products closer to market.

Because economy cars account for almost 60 percent of new cars sold in Brazil, the four companies are concentrating small-car production in that country and moving mid-size vehicle production to Argentina, analysts say.

For example, General Motors produces its Corsa sedan models in Argentina while its Brazilian plants assemble the Corsa economy model. Ford has adopted a similar strategy, assembling its compact Fiesta in Brazil and the mid-size Escort in Argentina.
